claim: DNA sequencing has revolutionized our ability to read genomes.
source: Advances in DNA sequencing have revolutionized our ability to read genomes.
evidence: This is a general statement about the impact of DNA sequencing technology, representing established scientific consensus in the field.

claim: For approximately 65% of promoters in E. coli, their regulation remains unknown.
source: However, even in the most well-studied of organisms, the bacterium Escherichia coli, for ≈65% of promoters we remain ignorant of their regulation.
evidence: The manuscript cites this specific percentage as a known fact about E. coli regulatory knowledge, supported by references to databases like RegulonDB.

claim: Reg-Seq produces a base pair resolution dissection of more than 100 E. coli promoters in 12 growth conditions.
source: We introduce a new method, Reg-Seq, that links massively parallel reporter assays with mass spectrometry to produce a base pair resolution dissection of more than a E. coli promoters in 12 growth conditions.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results obtained in the study, supported by the data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Reg-Seq recapitulates known regulatory information.
source: We demonstrate that the method recapitulates known regulatory information.
evidence: The manuscript presents comparisons with gold standard genes showing that Reg-Seq recovers known regulatory architectures, as shown in Figure 3 and Appendix 2.

claim: Reg-Seq examines regulatory architectures for more than 80 promoters which previously had no known regulatory information.
source: Then, we examine regulatory architectures for more than 80 promoters which previously had no known regulatory information.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Tables 1 and 2, which categorize the promoters studied and identify newly discovered binding sites.

claim: Reg-Seq identifies which transcription factors mediate regulation in many cases.
source: In many cases, we also identify which transcription factors mediate their regulation.
evidence: The manuscript describes using mass spectrometry and other methods to identify transcription factors, as shown in Figures 5, 7, and 8, and detailed in Table 2.

claim: RNA-Seq was launched as a new era technology by studies from 2008.
source: The advent of RNA-Seq (Lister et al., 2008; Nagalakshmi et al., 2008; Mortazavi et al., 2008) launched a new era in which sequencing could be used as an experimental read-out of the biophysically interesting counts of mRNA, rather than simply as a tool for collecting ever more complete organismal genomes.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to three foundational papers from 2008 that established RNA-Seq technology.

claim: Massively parallel reporter assays (MPRAs) have been used to study gene expression in a variety of contexts.
source: In contrast to whole genome screening sequencing approaches, such as Tn-Seq (Goodall et al., 2018) and ChIP-Seq (Gao et al., 2018), which give a coarse-grained view of gene essentiality and regulation respectively, another class of experiments known as massively parallel reporter assays (MPRA) have been used to study gene expression in a variety of contexts (Patwardhan et al., 2009; Kinney et al., 2010; Sharon et al., 2012; Patwardhan et al., 2012; Melnikov et al., 2012; Kwasnieski et al., 2012; Fulco et al., 2019; Kinney and McCandlish, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies that have used MPRA methods in different contexts.

claim: Kosuri et al., 2013 screened more than 10,000 combinations of promoter and ribosome-binding sites to assess their impact on gene expression levels.
source: One elegant study relevant to the bacterial case of interest here by Kosuri et al., 2013 screened more than 104 combinations of promoter and ribosome-binding sites (RBS) to assess their impact on gene expression levels.
evidence: This is a specific claim about a previous study, supported by citation to Kosuri et al., 2013.

claim: Sort-Seq uses fluorescence activated cell sorting combined with sequencing to identify specific locations of transcription factor binding in the genome.
source: Sort-Seq uses fluorescence activated cell sorting (FACS) based on changes in the fluorescence due to mutated promoters combined with sequencing to identify the specific locations of transcription factor binding in the genome.
evidence: This describes the Sort-Seq methodology developed by Kinney et al., 2010, as cited in the text.

claim: Sort-Seq provides a readout of how promoter sequences control the level of gene expression with single base-pair resolution.
source: Importantly, it also provides a readout of how promoter sequences control the level of gene expression with single base-pair resolution.
evidence: This is a description of the capabilities of Sort-Seq, based on the cited work by Kinney et al., 2010.

claim: Belliveau et al., 2018 illustrated how Sort-Seq used in conjunction with mass spectrometry can identify which transcription factors bind to a given binding site.
source: Earlier work from Belliveau et al., 2018 illustrated how Sort-Seq, used in conjunction with mass spectrometry, can be used to identify which transcription factors bind to a given binding site, thus enabling the mechanistic dissection of promoters which previously had no regulatory annotation.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by citation to Belliveau et al., 2018.

claim: The approach of Belliveau et al., 2018 was unable to readily tackle multiple genes at once.
source: However, a crucial drawback of the approach of Belliveau et al., 2018 is that while it is high-throughput at the level of a single gene and the number of promoter variants it accesses, it was unable to readily tackle multiple genes at once.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the previous method, based on the authors' assessment of Belliveau et al., 2018.

claim: For more than 65% of E. coli genes, we remain completely ignorant of how those genes are regulated.
source: Even in one of biology's best understood organisms, the bacterium Escherichia coli, for more than 65% of its genes, we remain completely ignorant of how those genes are regulated (Belliveau et al., 2018; Santos-Zavaleta et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Belliveau et al., 2018 and Santos-Zavaleta et al., 2019.

claim: Reg-Seq replaces the low-throughput, fluorescence-based Sort-Seq approach with a scalable, RNA-Seq based approach.
source: Here, we replace the low-throughput, fluorescence-based Sort-Seq approach with a scalable, RNA-Seq based approach that makes it possible to attack many promoters at once.
evidence: This describes the methodological innovation of the current study, as demonstrated by the experimental results presented.

claim: Reg-Seq uses mutual information as a metric to measure the information flow from the distribution of sequences to gene expression.
source: We generate a broad diversity of promoter sequences for each promoter of interest and use mutual information as a metric to measure the information flow from that distribution of sequences to gene expression.
evidence: This describes the analytical approach used in the study, as detailed in the Methods section and demonstrated in the information footprints throughout the manuscript.

claim: 113 E. coli genes were studied in this work.
source: To demonstrate our ability to perform Reg-Seq at scale, we report here our results for 113 E. coli genes, whose regulatory architectures (i.e. gene-by-gene distributions of transcription-factor-binding sites and identities of the transcription factors that bind those sites) were determined in parallel for multiple different growth conditions.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental scope, supported by the data presented in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: The regulatory architectures of 113 E. coli genes were determined in parallel for multiple different growth conditions.
source: To demonstrate our ability to perform Reg-Seq at scale, we report here our results for 113 E. coli genes, whose regulatory architectures (i.e. gene-by-gene distributions of transcription-factor-binding sites and identities of the transcription factors that bind those sites) were determined in parallel for multiple different growth conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript, including information footprints for different growth conditions.

claim: The field remains limited in its understanding of which specific growth conditions, small molecules and metabolites are responsible for altering the milieu of transcription factor activities.
source: Although we make substantial progress in mapping the regulatory information for a swath of E. coli genes in this study (the 'regulome'), the field still remains limited in its understanding of which specific growth conditions, small molecules and metabolites (the allosterome) are responsible for altering the milieu of transcription factor activities (Lindsley and Rutter, 2006; Piazza et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field, supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: The study explored more than 100 genes from across the E. coli genome.
source: As shown in Figure 1, we have explored more than 100 genes from across the E. coli genome.
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 1, which shows the genomic locations of the genes studied, and by the data in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: The set of gold standard genes includes lacZYA, znuCB, znuA, ompR, araC, marR, relBE, dgoR, dicC, ftsK, xylA, xylF, rspA, dicA, and araAB.
source: Our set of gold standard genes is lacZYA, znuCB, znuA, ompR, araC, marR, relBE, dgoR, dicC, ftsK, xylA, xylF, rspA, dicA, and araAB.
evidence: This is a direct listing of the gold standard genes used to validate the method.

claim: Reg-Seq recovers the regulatory elements of gold standard cases fully in 11 out of 15 cases.
source: We find that our method recovers the regulatory elements of these gold standard cases fully in 11 out of 15 cases, and the majority of regulatory elements in two of the remaining cases.
evidence: This is a quantitative assessment of the method's performance, supported by the detailed comparisons in Appendix 2.

claim: Genes were selected in part using data from a proteomic study by Schmidt et al., 2016.
source: These promoters of known regulatory architecture are complemented by an array of previously uncharacterized genes that we selected in part using data from a recent proteomic study, in which mass spectrometry was used to measure the copy number of different proteins in 22 distinct growth conditions (Schmidt et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the gene selection strategy, supported by citation to Schmidt et al., 2016.

claim: Genes that exhibited wide variation in copy number over different growth conditions were selected, reasoning that differential expression implies regulatory control.
source: We selected genes that exhibited a wide variation in their copy number over the different growth conditions considered, reasoning that differential expression across growth conditions implies that those genes are under regulatory control.
evidence: This describes the rationale for gene selection, based on logical inference from expression patterns.

claim: The original Sort-Seq formulation was based on fluorescence activated cell sorting, one gene at a time.
source: As noted in the introduction, the original formulation of Reg-Seq, termed Sort-Seq, was based on the use of fluorescence activated cell sorting, one gene at a time, as a way to uncover putative binding sites for previously uncharacterized promoters (Belliveau et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the previous methodology, supported by citation to Belliveau et al., 2018.

claim: In the Reg-Seq approach, each promoter variant is designed to express an mRNA with a unique sequence barcode.
source: In the Reg-Seq approach, for each promoter interrogated, we generate a library of mutated variants and design each variant to express an mRNA with a unique sequence barcode.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of Reg-Seq, as detailed in the Methods section and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: The frequency of each expressed barcode is counted using RNA-Seq to assess differential expression.
source: By counting the frequency of each expressed barcode using RNA-Seq, we can assess the differential expression from our promoter of interest based on the base-pair by base-pair sequence of its promoter.
evidence: This describes the measurement approach used in Reg-Seq, as detailed in the Methods section.

claim: Mutual information between mRNA counts and sequences is used to develop an information footprint.
source: Using the mutual information between mRNA counts and sequences, we develop an information footprint that reveals the importance of different bases in the promoter region to the overall level of expression.
evidence: This describes the analytical method used to generate information footprints, as shown throughout the manuscript.

claim: Potential transcription-factor-binding regions are located by looking for clusters of base pairs that have a significant effect on gene expression.
source: We locate potential transcription-factor-binding regions by looking for clusters of base pairs that have a significant effect on gene expression.
evidence: This describes the method for identifying binding sites from information footprints, as detailed in the Methods section.

claim: Blue regions in information footprints correspond to hypothesized activating sequences.
source: Blue regions of the histogram shown in the information footprints of Figure 2 correspond to hypothesized activating sequences and red regions of the histogram correspond to hypothesized repressing sequences.
evidence: This describes the color coding convention used in information footprints throughout the manuscript.

claim: Red regions in information footprints correspond to hypothesized repressing sequences.
source: Blue regions of the histogram shown in the information footprints of Figure 2 correspond to hypothesized activating sequences and red regions of the histogram correspond to hypothesized repressing sequences.
evidence: This describes the color coding convention used in information footprints throughout the manuscript.

claim: The dgoRKADT promoter is activated by CRP in the presence of galactonate.
source: The dgoRKADT promoter is activated by CRP in the presence of galactonate and is repressed by DgoR.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about the dgoRKADT promoter, used as a gold standard for comparison.

claim: The dgoRKADT promoter is repressed by DgoR.
source: The dgoRKADT promoter is activated by CRP in the presence of galactonate and is repressed by DgoR.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about the dgoRKADT promoter, used as a gold standard for comparison.

claim: The relBE promoter is repressed by RelBE.
source: The relBE promoter is repressed by RelBE as can be identified algorithmically in both Sort-Seq and Reg-Seq.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about the relBE promoter, used as a gold standard for comparison, and confirmed by both methods.

claim: The marRAB promoter is repressed by MarR.
source: The marRAB promoter is repressed by MarR.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about the marRAB promoter, used as a gold standard for comparison.

claim: The rightmost MarR site overlaps with a ribosome-binding site.
source: The right most MarR site overlaps with a ribosome-binding site.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the marRAB promoter architecture.

claim: Energy matrices are scaled such that the wild type sequence is colored in white, mutations that improve binding are shown in blue, and mutations that weaken binding are shown in red.
source: These energy matrices are scaled such that the wild type sequence is colored in white, mutations that improve binding are shown in blue, and mutations that weaken binding are shown in red.
evidence: This describes the color coding convention used for energy matrices throughout the manuscript.

claim: Energy matrices encode a full quantitative picture for how sequence relates to binding for a given transcription factor.
source: These energy matrices encode a full quantitative picture for how we expect sequence to relate to binding for a given transcription factor, such that we can provide a prediction for the binding energy of every possible binding site sequence
evidence: This describes the information content and utility of energy matrices, based on the linear binding model used.

claim: The ykgE promoter has a repressor-binding site downstream of the RNAP-binding site.
source: From the information footprint of the ykgE promoter under different growth conditions, we can identify a repressor-binding site downstream of the RNAP-binding site.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A through the information footprint analysis.

claim: YieP is the transcription factor bound to the repressor site in the ykgE promoter.
source: From the enrichment of proteins bound to the DNA sequence of the putative repressor as compared to a control sequence, we can identify YieP as the transcription factor bound to this site as it has a much higher enrichment ratio than any other protein.
evidence: This is demonstrated by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The wild-type sequence of the YieP binding site in ykgE is the strongest possible binder.
source: Lastly, the binding energy matrix for the repressor site along with corresponding sequence logo shows that the wild-type sequence is the strongest possible binder and it displays an imperfect inverted repeat symmetry.
evidence: This is shown in the energy matrix and sequence logo in Figure 5A.

claim: The YieP binding site in ykgE displays an imperfect inverted repeat symmetry.
source: Lastly, the binding energy matrix for the repressor site along with corresponding sequence logo shows that the wild-type sequence is the strongest possible binder and it displays an imperfect inverted repeat symmetry.
evidence: This is shown in the sequence logo in Figure 5A.

claim: YciT binds to the phnA promoter.
source: As shown in Figure 5, our study has found the first examples that we are aware of in the entire E. coli genome of a binding site for YciT.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the information footprint and mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The study found the first examples of binding sites for YciT in the entire E. coli genome.
source: As shown in Figure 5, our study has found the first examples that we are aware of in the entire E. coli genome of a binding site for YciT.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the YciT binding site discovery, based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: Of the 113 genes considered, 34 revealed no signature of any transcription-factor-binding sites and are labeled as (0, 0).
source: As seen in Table 1, of the 113 genes we considered, 34 of them revealed no signature of any transcription-factor-binding sites and they are labeled as (0, 0).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results presented in Table 1.

claim: The simple repression architecture (0, 1) was found 26 times.
source: The simple repression architecture (0, 1) was found 26 times, the simple activation architecture (1, 0) was found 11 times, and more complex architectures featuring multiple binding sites (e.g. (1, 1), (0, 2), (2, 0), etc.) were revealed as well.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results presented in Table 1 and Figure 6.

claim: The simple activation architecture (1, 0) was found 11 times.
source: The simple repression architecture (0, 1) was found 26 times, the simple activation architecture (1, 0) was found 11 times, and more complex architectures featuring multiple binding sites (e.g. (1, 1), (0, 2), (2, 0), etc.) were revealed as well.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results presented in Table 1 and Figure 6.

claim: For 18 genes labeled 'inactive', Reg-Seq did not reveal a potential RNAP-binding site.
source: Further, for 18 of the genes that we label 'inactive', Reg-Seq did not reveal a potential RNAP-binding site.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results presented in Table 1.

claim: The lack of observable RNAP site could be because the proper growth condition to get high levels of expression was not used, or because the mutation window chosen for the gene does not capture a highly transcribing TSS.
source: The lack of observable RNAP site could be because the proper growth condition to get high levels of expression was not used, or because the mutation window chosen for the gene does not capture a highly transcribing TSS.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for why some genes appeared inactive, based on the authors' understanding of the method's limitations.

claim: The most common motif to emerge from the work (with the exception of constitutive expression) is the simple repression motif.
source: We observe that the most common motif to emerge from our work (with the exception of constitutive expression) is the simple repression motif.
evidence: This is an observation based on the data presented in Table 1 and Figure 6.

claim: The newly discovered binding sites for GlpR more than double the number of operons known to be regulated by GlpR as reported in RegulonDB.
source: The newly discovered binding sites in Figure 7(A), with additional evidence for GlpR binding in Figure 7(B) and (C), more than double the number of operons known to be regulated by GlpR as reported in RegulonDB (Santos-Zavaleta et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim compares the new discoveries to the existing database, supported by citation to RegulonDB.

claim: Five newly regulated operons by GlpR were found in the dataset.
source: We found five newly regulated operons in our data set, even though we were not specifically targeting GlpR regulation.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results shown in Figure 7.

claim: Finding five GlpR-regulated operons out of approximately 100 examined operons supports the claim that GlpR widely regulates and many more of its sites would be found in a full search of the genome.
source: Although the number of example promoters across the genome that we considered is too small to make good estimates, finding five regulated operons out of approximately 100 examined operons supports the claim that GlpR widely regulates and many more of its sites would be found in a full search of the genome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the frequency of GlpR sites found in the sample of promoters studied.

claim: The regulatory roles revealed in Figure 7(A) reinforce the evidence that GlpR is a repressor.
source: The regulatory roles revealed in Figure 7(A) also reinforce the evidence that GlpR is a repressor.
evidence: This is an inference based on the information footprints shown in Figure 7A, where mutations in GlpR binding sites increase expression.

claim: For the GlpR-regulated operons newly discovered, GlpR binds strongly in the presence of glucose while all other growth conditions result in greatly diminished, but not entirely abolished, binding.
source: For the GlpR-regulated operons newly discovered here, we found that this repressor binds strongly in the presence of glucose while all other growth conditions result in greatly diminished, but not entirely abolished, binding (Figure 7(A)).
evidence: This is an observation based on the information footprints shown in Figure 7A for different growth conditions.

claim: There is no previously known direct molecular interaction between GlpR and glucose.
source: As there is no previously known direct molecular interaction between GlpR and glucose and the repression is reduced but not eliminated, the derepression in the absence of glucose is likely an indirect effect.
evidence: This is a statement about the existing knowledge in the literature regarding GlpR-glucose interactions.

claim: The derepression of GlpR in the absence of glucose is likely an indirect effect.
source: As there is no previously known direct molecular interaction between GlpR and glucose and the repression is reduced but not eliminated, the derepression in the absence of glucose is likely an indirect effect.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on the observation that GlpR binding changes with glucose but there is no known direct interaction.

claim: gpsA is known to be activated by CRP.
source: As a potential mechanism of the indirect effect, gpsA is known to be activated by CRP (Seoh and Tai, 1999), and GpsA is involved in the synthesis of glycerol-3-phosphate (G3P), a known binding partner of GlpR which disables its repressive activity (Larson et al., 1987).
evidence: This is a known fact from the literature, supported by citation to Seoh and Tai, 1999.

claim: GpsA is involved in the synthesis of glycerol-3-phosphate (G3P).
source: As a potential mechanism of the indirect effect, gpsA is known to be activated by CRP (Seoh and Tai, 1999), and GpsA is involved in the synthesis of glycerol-3-phosphate (G3P), a known binding partner of GlpR which disables its repressive activity (Larson et al., 1987).
evidence: This is a known fact from the literature, supported by citation to Larson et al., 1987.

claim: G3P is a known binding partner of GlpR which disables its repressive activity.
source: As a potential mechanism of the indirect effect, gpsA is known to be activated by CRP (Seoh and Tai, 1999), and GpsA is involved in the synthesis of glycerol-3-phosphate (G3P), a known binding partner of GlpR which disables its repressive activity (Larson et al., 1987).
evidence: This is a known fact from the literature, supported by citation to Larson et al., 1987.

claim: In the presence of glucose, GpsA and consequently G3P will be found at low concentrations, ultimately allowing GlpR to fulfill its role as a repressor.
source: Thus, in the presence of glucose, GpsA and consequently G3P will be found at low concentrations, ultimately allowing GlpR to fulfill its role as a repressor.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation inferred from the known regulatory relationships and the observed glucose-dependent GlpR binding.

claim: Prior to this study, there were four operons known to be regulated by GlpR, each with between 4 and 8 GlpR-binding sites.
source: Prior to this study, there were four operons known to be regulated by GlpR, each with between 4 and 8 GlpR-binding sites (Larson et al., 1992; Zhao et al., 1994; Yang and Larson, 1996; Ye and Larson, 1988; Weissenborn et al., 1992), where the absence of glucose and the partial induction of GlpR was not enough to prompt a notable change in gene expression (Lin, 1976).
evidence: This is a summary of prior knowledge from the literature, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The previously explored GlpR-regulated operons seemingly are regulated as part of an AND gate.
source: These previously explored operons seemingly are regulated as part of an AND gate.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the regulatory logic based on the cited literature.

claim: glpTQ, glpRABC, glpD, and glpFKX have high gene expression when grown in growth media that does not contain glucose but does contain G3P (or glycerol).
source: glpTQ, glpRABC, glpD, and glpFKX have high gene expression when grown in growth media that does not contain glucose but does contain contain G3P (or glycerol, which leads to high concentrations of G3P).
evidence: This is a known fact from the literature, supported by citation to Lin, 1976.

claim: The study discovered operons whose regulation appears to be mediated by a single GlpR site per operon.
source: In contrast, we have discovered operons whose regulation appears to be mediated by a single GlpR site per operon.
evidence: This is a summary of the new findings shown in Figure 7, contrasting with previously known GlpR-regulated operons.

claim: With only a single GlpR site, GlpR functions as an indirect glucose sensor, as only the absence of glucose is needed to relieve repression by GlpR.
source: With only a single site, GlpR functions as an indirect glucose sensor, as only the absence of glucose is needed to relieve repression by GlpR.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the regulatory mechanism based on the observed glucose-dependent binding patterns.

claim: FNR has 151 binding sites already reported in RegulonDB.
source: The second widely acting regulator our study revealed, FNR, has 151 binding sites already reported in RegulonDB and is well studied compared to most transcription factors (Santos-Zavaleta et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a fact from the RegulonDB database, supported by citation to Santos-Zavaleta et al., 2019.

claim: FNR is well studied compared to most transcription factors.
source: The second widely acting regulator our study revealed, FNR, has 151 binding sites already reported in RegulonDB and is well studied compared to most transcription factors (Santos-Zavaleta et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about the relative state of knowledge regarding FNR, based on the database information.

claim: The newly discovered FNR sites demonstrate that even for well-understood transcription factors there is much still to be uncovered.
source: However, the newly discovered FNR sites displayed in Figure 8(A), with sequence logos of the respective sites displayed in Figure 8(B), demonstrate that even for well-understood transcription factors there is much still to be uncovered.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the discovery of new FNR binding sites despite FNR being well-studied.

claim: Information footprints are in agreement with previous studies suggesting that FNR acts as an activator.
source: Our information footprints are in agreement with previous studies suggesting that FNR acts as an activator.
evidence: This compares the current findings to previous literature on FNR function.

claim: In the presence of O2, dimeric FNR is converted to a monomeric form and its ability to bind DNA is greatly reduced.
source: In the presence of O2, dimeric FNR is converted to a monomeric form and its ability to bind DNA is greatly reduced (Myers et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a known fact from the literature, supported by citation to Myers et al., 2013.

claim: Only in low oxygen conditions was a binding signature from FNR observed.
source: Only in low oxygen conditions did we observe a binding signature from FNR, and we show a representative example of the information footprint from one of 11 aerobic growth conditions in Figure 8(A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: FNR affects the expression of fdhE both directly through transcription factor binding and indirectly through increased expression of ArcA.
source: We observe quantitatively how FNR affects the expression of fdhE both directly through transcription factor binding (Figure 9B and C) and indirectly through increased expression of ArcA (Figure 9A, B, C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 9, showing FNR binding to both arcA and fdhE promoters.

claim: 36% of all multi-gene operons have at least one TSS which transcribes only a subset of the genes in the operon.
source: 36% of all multi-gene operons have at least one TSS which transcribes only a subset of the genes in the operon (Conway et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a fact from the literature, supported by citation to Conway et al., 2014.

claim: Regulation within an operon is even more poorly studied than regulation in general.
source: Regulation within an operon is even more poorly studied than regulation in general.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, based on the authors' assessment of the literature.

claim: The main promoter for fdoGHI-fdhE has a repressor-binding site.
source: The main promoter for fdoGHI-fdhE has a repressor-binding site, which demonstrates that there is regulatory control of the entire operon.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experimental data.

claim: fdhE is regulated by both ArcA and FNR and will therefore be upregulated in anaerobic conditions.
source: However, we also see in Figure 9(B) that there is control at the promoter level, as fdhE is regulated by both ArcA and FNR and will therefore be upregulated in anaerobic conditions (Compan and Touati, 1994).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 9B and supported by citation to Compan and Touati, 1994.

claim: The main TSS of fdoGHI-fdhE transcribes all four genes in the operon.
source: The main TSS transcribes all four genes in the operon, while the secondary site shown in Figure 9(B) only transcribes fdhE, and therefore anaerobic conditions will change the stoichiometry of the proteins produced by the operon.
evidence: This is an observation about the operon structure and its regulatory implications.

claim: The secondary TSS shown in Figure 9(B) only transcribes fdhE.
source: The main TSS transcribes all four genes in the operon, while the secondary site shown in Figure 9(B) only transcribes fdhE, and therefore anaerobic conditions will change the stoichiometry of the proteins produced by the operon.
evidence: This is an observation about the operon structure shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Anaerobic conditions will change the stoichiometry of the proteins produced by the fdoGHI-fdhE operon.
source: The main TSS transcribes all four genes in the operon, while the secondary site shown in Figure 9(B) only transcribes fdhE, and therefore anaerobic conditions will change the stoichiometry of the proteins produced by the operon.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential regulation of the two TSSs in the operon.

claim: By examining over 100 promoters grown under 12 growth conditions, there is a total of more than 1000 information footprints and data sets.
source: By examining the over 100 promoters considered here, grown under 12 growth conditions, we have a total of more than 1000 information footprints and data sets.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the number of promoters and growth conditions studied.

claim: An online resource has been developed that makes it possible for anyone to view the data and draw their own biological conclusions.
source: To that end, as introduced in Figure 10, we have developed an online resource (see https://www.rpgroup.caltech.edu/RegSeq/interactive) that makes it possible for anyone who is interested to view our data and draw their own biological conclusions.
evidence: This describes the availability of an online resource for data exploration.

claim: The interactive figure was invaluable in identifying transcription factors whose binding properties vary depending on growth condition.
source: The interactive figure in question was invaluable in identifying transcription factors, such as GlpR, whose binding properties vary depending on growth condition.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of the interactive figure in the analysis process.

claim: Studying the interactive figure identified many of the secondary RNAP sites present.
source: As sigma factor availability also varies greatly depending on growth condition, studying the interactive figure identified many of the secondary RNAP sites present.
evidence: This is a statement about how the interactive figure aided in identifying secondary RNAP sites.

claim: Roughly 35% of the genes in E. coli lack experimental evidence of function.
source: Previously christened as the 'y-ome', Ghatak et al., 2019 surprisingly found that roughly 35% of the genes in E. coli lack experimental evidence of function.
evidence: This is a fact from the literature, supported by citation to Ghatak et al., 2019.

claim: The situation regarding unknown gene function is likely worse for organisms other than E. coli.
source: The situation is likely worse for other organisms.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on E. coli being one of the best-studied organisms.

claim: Reg-Seq is not fully automated for various aspects in the experimental pipeline.
source: First, the current implementation of Reg-Seq is not fully automated for various aspects in the experimental pipeline; for example, manual examination of information footprints is used to generate testable regulatory hypotheses.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the current method.

claim: Manual examination of information footprints is used to generate testable regulatory hypotheses.
source: First, the current implementation of Reg-Seq is not fully automated for various aspects in the experimental pipeline; for example, manual examination of information footprints is used to generate testable regulatory hypotheses.
evidence: This describes the current analysis workflow.

claim: An automated methodology for identifying putative binding sites has been created.
source: To address this for future work, we have created an automated methodology for identifying putative binding sites, which we describe in the Materials and methods section, that will simplify future scaled up efforts at identifying putative binding sites.
evidence: This describes a methodological development presented in the manuscript.

claim: All putative binding sites reported in this study either were identified through the automated methodology or have additional evidence for their presence such as mass spectrometry.
source: All putative binding sites reported in this study either were identified through the automated methodology or have additional evidence for their presence such as mass spectrometry.
evidence: This describes the validation criteria for reported binding sites.

claim: The mass spectrometry and gene knockout confirmation aspects of the experimental pipeline remain low-throughput and, at times, inconclusive.
source: Another key challenge faced by the methods described here is that the mass spectrometry and the gene knockout confirmation aspects of the experimental pipeline remain low-throughput and, at times, inconclusive.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the current method.

claim: It has been found challenging to observe weaker binding sites when multiple strong binding sites are also present.
source: Occasionally, we have found it challenging to observe weaker binding sites when multiple strong binding sites are also present.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the method, illustrated by the marRAB example.

claim: The study is exploring multiplexed mass spectrometry measurements and multiplexed Reg-Seq on libraries of gene knockouts as ways to break the identification bottleneck.
source: Specifically, we are exploring multiplexed mass spectrometry measurements and multiplexed Reg-Seq on libraries of gene knockouts as ways to break the identification bottleneck.
evidence: This describes future directions for improving the method.

claim: Information on the location of a TSS is available for 2500 of 2600 operons in E. coli.
source: While information on the location of a TSS is available for 2500 of 2600 operons in E. coli (Santos-Zavaleta et al., 2019), this information does not guarantee those sites will have high transcription in the growth conditions studied.
evidence: This is a fact from the RegulonDB database, supported by citation to Santos-Zavaleta et al., 2019.

claim: Many genes have multiple TSS that can be active under different growth conditions.
source: Similarly, many genes have multiple TSS that can be active under different growth conditions.
evidence: This is a known fact about bacterial gene regulation.

claim: The current implementation of Reg-Seq misses regulatory action at a distance.
source: Another shortcoming of the current implementation of the method is that it misses regulatory action at a distance.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the method.

claim: Transcriptional control through enhancers in eukaryotic regulation is central in contexts ranging from embryonic development to hematopoiesis.
source: It is well known that transcriptional control through enhancers in eukaryotic regulation is central in contexts ranging from embryonic development to hematopoiesis (Melnikov et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a known fact about eukaryotic gene regulation, supported by citation.

claim: The current incarnation of the methods has focused on contiguous regions in the vicinity of the transcription start site (within the 160 base pair mutagenized window).
source: The current incarnation of the methods, as described here, have focused on contiguous regions in the vicinity of the transcription start site (within the 160 base pair mutagenized window).
evidence: This describes the scope of the current method.

claim: 113 TSS from the E. coli K12 genome were selected for experiments.
source: We selected 113 TSS from the E. coli K12 genome for experiments.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The promoter regions analyzed in this study were each 160 base pairs in length.
source: The promoter regions analyzed in this study were each 160 base pairs in length, a region that includes 45 base pairs downstream and 115 base pairs upstream of each TSS.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Each promoter region includes 45 base pairs downstream and 115 base pairs upstream of each TSS.
source: The promoter regions analyzed in this study were each 160 base pairs in length, a region that includes 45 base pairs downstream and 115 base pairs upstream of each TSS.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Promoter variants were synthesized on a microarray by TWIST Bioscience.
source: Promoter variants were synthesized on a microarray (TWIST Bioscience, San Francisco, CA).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods.

claim: The sequences were designed computationally such that each base in the 160 base pair promoter region has a 10% probability of being mutated.
source: The sequences were designed computationally such that each base in the 160 base pair promoter region has a 10% probability of being mutated.
evidence: This describes the experimental design for library construction.

claim: There are an average of 2200 unique promoter sequences per gene.
source: There are an average of 2200 unique promoter sequences per gene (for an analysis of how our results depend upon number of unique promoter sequences see Appendix 3—figure 1).
evidence: This describes the library complexity, with reference to an analysis in the appendix.

claim: All genetic barcodes were inserted 120 base pairs from the 5' end of the mRNA.
source: All genetic barcodes were inserted 120 base pairs from the 5' end of the mRNA, containing 45 base pairs from the targeted regulatory region, 64 base pairs containing primer sites used in the construction of the plasmid, and 11 base pairs containing a three frame stop codon.
evidence: This describes the construct design.

claim: Cells were grown to an optical density of 0.3 before RNA stabilization.
source: To prepare cDNA libraries for sequencing, cells were grown to an optical density of 0.3 and RNA was stabilized using Qiagen RNA Protect (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: An average of five unique 20 base pair barcodes per variant promoter was used for the purpose of counting transcripts.
source: An average of five unique 20 base pair barcodes per variant promoter was used for the purpose of counting transcripts.
evidence: This describes the experimental design for transcript counting.

claim: Energy matrices are inferred by maximizing the mutual information between the rank-ordered binding strength predictions from the energy matrix and the gene expression data.
source: We use relative gene expression values, as determined by counting genetic barcodes from NGS data for each mutated variant of a given regulatory sequence, and infer the energy contribution of each nucleotide by maximizing the mutual information between the rank-ordered binding strength predictions from the energy matrix and the gene expression data.
evidence: This describes the computational method for inferring energy matrices.

claim: MCMC is used to perform the maximization for energy matrix inference.
source: We also perform this maximization using MCMC.
evidence: This describes the computational method used.

claim: Biotinylated oligos of binding sites of interest are ordered along with a control 'scrambled' sequence.
source: In brief, we order biotinylated oligos of our binding site of interest (Integrated DNA Technologies, Coralville, IA) along with a control, 'scrambled' sequence, that we expect to have no specificity for the given transcription factor.
evidence: This describes the DNA-affinity chromatography protocol.

claim: Oligos are tethered to magnetic streptavidin beads and incubated overnight with whole cell lysate.
source: We tether these oligos to magnetic streptavidin beads (Dynabeads MyOne T1; ThermoFisher, Waltham, MA), and incubate them overnight with whole cell lysate grown in the presences of either heavy (with 15N) or light (with 14N) lysine for the experimental and control sequences, respectively.
evidence: This describes the DNA-affinity chromatography protocol.

claim: Only a subset (13) of all transcription factor targets were identified by mass spectrometry due to limitations in scaling the technique to large numbers of targets.
source: Only a subset (13) of all transcription factor targets were identified by mass spectrometry due to limitations in scaling the technique to large numbers of targets.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the mass spectrometry approach.

claim: The transcription factors identified by mass spectrometry are enriched more than any other DNA binding protein, with p<0.01.
source: The transcription factors identified by this method are enriched more than any other DNA binding protein, with p<0.01 using the outlier detection method as outlined by Cox and Mann, 2008, with corrections for multiple hypothesis testing using the method proposed by Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995.
evidence: This describes the statistical criteria for transcription factor identification.

claim: Knockout strains were ordered from the Keio collection.
source: To construct the knockout strains, we ordered strains from the Keio collection (Yamamoto et al., 2009) from the Coli Genetic Stock Center.
evidence: This describes the source of knockout strains used.

claim: A Pearson correlation coefficient threshold of 0.45 is used to identify RNAP-binding site locations.
source: We find RNAP-binding site locations by thresholding the Pearson correlation coefficients at a value of 0.45.
evidence: This describes the automated RNAP site identification method.

claim: During manual curation of binding sites, any binding sites where there are only three or fewer base pairs with high values in the mutual information footprint are disqualified.
source: During manual curation of binding sites, we also disqualify any binding sites where there are only three or fewer base pairs with high values in the mutual information footprint.
evidence: This describes the manual curation criteria.
